title: Frog Jump
description:
# Frog Jump

A frog wants to cross a river by landing only on stones. The stones are given as a strictly increasing array `stones`, where `stones[i]` is the position of the `i`th stone.

The frog starts on `stones[0]`, which is always position `0`. Its first jump must be exactly `1` unit. After the frog makes a jump of length `k`, its next jump may have length `k - 1`, `k`, or `k + 1`.

The frog may only jump forward, and it may land only on positions that contain stones. Return `true` if the frog can land on the last stone, otherwise return `false`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** stones = [0,1,3,5,6,8,12,17]

**Output:** true

**Explanation:** One valid route uses jump lengths 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

## Example 2:

**Input:** stones = [0,1,2,3,4,8,9,11]

**Output:** false

**Explanation:** After the early stones, the gap to position 8 is too large for any valid previous jump length.

## Constraints:

* `2 <= stones.length <= 2000`
* `0 <= stones[i] <= 2^31 - 1`
* `stones[0] == 0`
* `stones` is sorted in strictly increasing order.

solutions.name: Position-to-Jump Set DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Create a map from each stone position to the set of jump lengths that can land on that stone. Start with jump length `0` at position `0`, then propagate `k - 1`, `k`, and `k + 1` to later stones when those positions exist.

## Key Insight

The complete state is not just the stone position. The last jump length controls the next legal moves, so each stone must remember every last jump size that can reach it.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Stone-Pair Dynamic Programming
solutions.description:
## Approach

Let `dp[i][k]` mean that the frog can land on stone `i` with a last jump of length `k`. For each pair of stones `j < i`, compute `jump = stones[i] - stones[j]` and check whether stone `j` was reachable with `jump - 1`, `jump`, or `jump + 1`.

## Key Insight

Instead of pushing states forward, this route asks whether the last jump into the current stone could have come from each earlier stone. It makes the recurrence behind the state graph explicit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: DFS Memo on Stone and Jump
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use recursive search on `(stoneIndex, lastJump)`. A hash map converts a target position into its stone index, and a memo table stores whether each state can eventually reach the final stone.

## Key Insight

The same stone and last jump may be reached through several routes. Once that state is solved, the answer is independent of the path used to get there, so memoization removes the exponential branching.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: BFS over Reachable States
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat every `(stoneIndex, lastJump)` pair as a node in a graph. Start from `(0, 0)`, use a queue to explore valid next jumps, and mark visited states so the same pair is not processed twice.

## Key Insight

This is the same state space as DFS memoization, but breadth-first traversal makes it clear that the task is reachability in a finite directed graph of legal frog states.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: BitSet Jump Sets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use one `BitSet` per stone. Bit `k` in `reachable[i]` means that stone `i` can be reached with a last jump length of `k`. Iterate over the set bits and propagate the next legal jump lengths to later stones.

## Key Insight

The set-DP idea can be stored more compactly when jump lengths are bounded by the number of stones. A `BitSet` keeps the same states while avoiding many small hash-set allocations.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)
